paragraphs: One-sentence assessment | This career is worth exploring further only if you are willing to operate equipment according to procedures over the long term in workshops, on site or in testing rooms, uphold safety requirements amid noise, radiation and outdoor conditions, and document the applicable standards and review records for every interpretation.

Core output | Connect the inspected object, method, equipment and parameters, original signals or images, applicable standards and interpretations into a traceable inspection report: judgments on defect location and nature, acceptance or rejection conclusions, limitations and escalation recommendations, rather than just a result.

20—120-minute safe trial | Conduct an off-site exercise using public teaching images or fictional data: explain the selected inspection method and reasons, create column headings for a calibration and parameter record, mark two potential defects and state the applicable standards and review requirements. Do not use this exercise to release or reject any real component.

First hurdle | Verify authorization boundaries first: who may operate radiation devices, evaluate results and sign reports. Nondestructive testing of special equipment in mainland China requires a Special Equipment Inspection and Testing Personnel Certificate (Nondestructive Testing Personnel), classified by method and levels Ⅰ / Ⅱ / Ⅲ. Level Ⅰ personnel may only operate and record under guidance. Work such as using mobile gamma radiography equipment additionally requires intermediate or advanced radiation safety training.

Non-destructive testing specialists (O*NET-SOC 17-3029.01) inspect structures and equipment for defects without damaging the inspected object. They select, calibrate and operate ultrasonic, radiographic, magnetic particle, penetrant, eddy current and acoustic emission testing equipment according to standards, codes and procedures; interpret signals and images and evaluate results against codes; document methods and processes and prepare inspection reports; and meet radiation and on-site work safety requirements.

entries: Method selection and equipment calibration | Select inspection methods according to the object, material and standards, calibrate or operate equipment and record parameters.

Nondestructive testing | Perform ultrasonic, radiographic, magnetic particle, penetrant, eddy current, acoustic emission, visual or thermal imaging inspections, including visual examinations assisted by borescopes and closed-circuit television.
Signal and image interpretation | Interpret results from different methods and evaluate defect nature and location against applicable codes, standards, specifications or procedures.
Result recording and reporting | Document inspection methods, procedures and results, and prepare nondestructive testing reports.
Objects covered | Inspect structures or vehicles such as aircraft, trains, nuclear reactors, bridges, dams and pipelines.
Guidance and collaboration | Supervise or guide nondestructive testing trainees and employees, and support project communications with clients or regulators.

paragraphs: Work primarily takes place on site and in workshops. O*NET work context data show that 23% are exposed to radiation daily, 32% wear specialized protective equipment daily, 77% wear common protective equipment daily, 32% are exposed to noise daily, and 14% work outdoors without shelter daily. Meanwhile, 77% have irregular schedules and 73% work more than 40 hours per week.

Accuracy and safety responsibilities are both high: 59% consider exactness or accuracy extremely important, 38% report extremely serious consequences of errors, 41% hold very high responsibility for others' health and safety, and 45% consider decision outcomes very important to the company. Decision-making freedom is primarily substantial freedom at 41% or some freedom at 36%.

The emphasis is on matching methods to standards: linking objects, materials, geometry and defect types to suitable methods and parameters, and explaining why the method's detection capability and limitations fit the inspection.

Quality is measured by traceable method selection and applicable standards, complete calibration and parameter records, reviewable original signals or images, explicit limitations and areas that cannot be inspected, and abnormalities and nonconformities escalated under procedures, rather than inspection volume.

Responsibility boundaries | Method, level, employer authorization and project signing authority are distinct statuses. Certification does not permit release of any object. Level Ⅰ personnel operate and record under guidance, level Ⅱ personnel may perform inspections and evaluate results, and level Ⅲ personnel handle procedures and reviews. Radiographic work must also meet radiation safety training and retraining requirements. Employer authorization and client or regulator acceptance conditions impose further constraints.

Quality inspectors and testing technicians | Focus on dimensional, appearance and routine performance inspections, typically without responsibility for interpreting radiographic or ultrasonic results or signing reports. This occupation centers on performing, interpreting and reporting multiple nondestructive testing methods.

Welding inspectors | Focus on welding processes and visual quality inspections and may use surface methods such as penetrant and magnetic particle testing. This occupation covers volumetric, acoustic and electromagnetic methods, with corresponding equipment and radiation safety requirements.

Selection signal | Compare more than the fact that all these roles inspect things. Consider the methods used, whether radiation sources or regulated objects such as pressure vessels are involved, and who evaluates results and signs reports.
Focuses on dimensional and visual inspections and judgments of process conformity, typically without responsibility for interpreting radiographic or ultrasonic volumetric testing.

Consider quality inspection if you prefer routine quality checks and process verification. Consider this occupation if you want responsibility for interpreting multiple methods and signing reports and are willing to accept radiation safety and qualification-level requirements.

Start with tasks | Task exposure to generative AI does not equal actual adoption, the probability of automation or job disappearance. The ILO's 2025 report states that approximately one-quarter of workers globally are in occupations with some exposure, but jobs are more likely to be reorganized than disappear outright because most tasks still require human input. This page analyzes tasks and work contexts from O*NET 17-3029.01 individually and does not invent a replacement rate.

Potential assistance (editorial analysis) | In authorized settings, assistance with procedure drafts, standards searches, records and formatting checks may be evaluated. Defect annotation requires dedicated validation of inspection algorithms; the Hot Technologies list does not establish generative models' inspection performance.

Digital inspection assistance | Built-in analysis functions in equipment such as phased-array and digital imaging systems may assist imaging and localization. Qualified personnel must still judge parameter settings, coverage and defect evaluation according to standards and procedures.

Conditional editorial recommendation | Rule-based checks may inspect parameters and missing fields. This review did not obtain evidence of actual deployment, false-positive rates or generative AI effects; tools cannot replace original signals or on-site interpretation.
Do not delegate to AI | Evaluating defect nature and acceptance conclusions, signing inspection reports, deciding release or repair, or determining radiation protection measures and work schedules.

Human control points | Verify the object and inspection scope, confirm the method and standard version, check equipment calibration status, have qualified personnel evaluate and sign results, and escalate abnormalities and nonconformities under procedures.

Before using data, verify its classification, contracts and client authorization. Handle confidential information involving nuclear power, national defense and similar fields under applicable rules, without labeling all public teaching dimensions and images secret or controlled. Do not upload unauthorized materials.

Capability development | Build knowledge of method principles and standards application, equipment operation and calibration, defect interpretation and limitation statements, on-site safety and radiation protection, beyond generating reports faster.

Name and scope | This occupation corresponds to O*NET-SOC 17-3029.01 (Non-Destructive Testing Specialists). In mainland China's special equipment sector, the Rules for Qualification of Special Equipment Nondestructive Testing Personnel (TSG Z8001—2019) apply. Methods include radiographic, ultrasonic, magnetic particle, penetrant, acoustic emission, eddy current and magnetic flux leakage testing, with levels Ⅰ, Ⅱ and Ⅲ. A Special Equipment Inspection and Testing Personnel Certificate (Nondestructive Testing Personnel) is required for the corresponding work.

Definition comparison | The National Bureau of Statistics publishes average wages of employees in urban units by industry section, without listing nondestructive testing specialists separately. This page uses averages for scientific research and technical services as a reference, with manufacturing averages also provided.

Verifiable reference | In 2025, average annual wages for employees in urban nonprivate units in scientific research and technical services were RMB 182,064, compared with RMB 83,560 in urban private units in the same industry. Manufacturing averages were RMB 113,594 for nonprivate units and RMB 76,055 for private units. Coverage includes legal entities in urban areas with 5 or more employees; individually owned businesses and freelancers are excluded.

Insufficient evidence: this review did not obtain a corresponding national Chinese occupational wage distribution. Scientific research and technical services and manufacturing averages serve only as references for related employers and do not establish occupational medians or individual income. From 2020, personnel take platform assessments under Ministry of Ecology and Environment Announcement No. 57 of 2019. The old four-year training certificate rule cannot be treated as a uniform requirement for all new personnel. Under Announcement No. 9 of 2021, personnel engaged only in selling or using category Ⅲ radiation devices are assessed by their own organizations, with results valid for five years and retraining and reassessment at expiry. Verify specific platform and score report requirements for other categories.

The 2025 BLS OEWS data displayed by O*NET use the combined occupation "Engineering Technologists and Technicians, Except Drafters, All Other (17-3029)": median hourly wage of USD 37.67 and median annual wage of USD 78,350. This category includes the other engineering technician category containing this occupation; it is not a separate value for 17-3029.01.

National annual wage percentiles under the same definition are USD 47,030 at the 10th percentile, USD 60,390 at the 25th, USD 99,310 at the 75th and USD 118,330 at the 90th. Corresponding hourly wages are USD 22.61, 29.03, 47.75 and 56.89.
The percentiles and medians all use 2025 BLS OEWS national data for a combined occupational category and cannot be directly compared across years, regions or method levels.

OEWS measures pretax wages for regular working hours and excludes the self-employed and owners / partners of unincorporated businesses. It includes hazard pay, incentives and production bonuses, while excluding overtime, shift differentials and lodging or meal payments, among other items. It does not categorically exclude all on-site or variable compensation.
Lower percentiles are not starting salaries for apprentices or newcomers, and distribution data cannot be used to estimate individual take-home pay or after-tax income.

Industries differ substantially: qualification and allowance structures in nuclear power, oil and gas and aerospace projects differ from routine manufacturing inspection. Verify the specific industry, employer and project conditions. US figures cannot be converted into individual income in mainland China.

Verification method | Personality and interest labels cannot determine fit. Use public teaching images to practice method selection and interpretation, and obtain evaluation from qualified personnel in a compliant teaching environment.

Scope statement | This checklist cannot replace institutional radiation safety policies, special equipment work requirements, on-site work permits or client and regulator rules. Main risks include incorrect method selection or standards application, missing calibration and parameter records, misinterpreted or missed defects, inadequate radiation and on-site safety measures, and signing conclusions beyond method levels or authorization. Controls should be tailored to the method, industry and jurisdiction.

Direct answer | The main risks are missed defects from methods or standards unsuitable for the object, unreviewable conclusions because parameter and calibration records are missing, incorrect judgments of defect nature and dimensions, interpretation bias amid noise and fatigue, radiation protection omissions during radiographic work, and acceptance conclusions beyond qualifications or authorization. Controls depend on procedural work, independent review, dose monitoring and safety briefings.

Evidence scope | Risk items derive from O*NET 17-3029.01 tasks and work contexts: 59% consider accuracy extremely important, 38% report extremely serious error consequences, 41% hold very high responsibility for others' health and safety, and 23% face daily radiation exposure. They also draw on method / level and responsibility distinctions in TSG Z8001—2019 and Ministry of Ecology and Environment radiation safety training and retraining requirements. Controls should be tailored to the method, industry and jurisdiction.

Method selection, operating records, interpretation and report signing, and on-site / radiation / quality roles may all be affected. Insufficient guidance may cause errors; comparative evidence that level Ⅰ personnel are most likely to err was not obtained.

Possible consequences | Missed or misinterpreted defects may cause pressure vessels, pipelines, bridges and rail components to fail, endangering public safety. Inadequate radiation protection may lead to excessive occupational exposure. Missing records may prevent review of conclusions and tracing of responsibility.

Job requirement sample (editorial compilation) | This page does not reproduce any single employer's job announcement. The following sample points derive from O*NET tasks and industry practices to help explain actual requirements and do not represent open vacancies. Typical requirements include familiarity with operation and recording for at least one nondestructive testing method, ability to interpret results against standards and prepare reports, acceptance of on-site work and travel, and responsibility for evaluation and signing after obtaining the relevant qualifications. Different industries may add radiation safety training, industry-specific codes or confidentiality requirements.

components.definition_block: Nondestructive testing specialists (O*NET-SOC 17-3029.01) use radiographic, ultrasonic, magnetic particle, penetrant, eddy current, acoustic emission, visual and thermal imaging methods to inspect the safety of structures, vehicles or equipment without damaging the inspected object. Work includes selecting and calibrating equipment, performing inspections, interpreting signals and images, evaluating results against codes, documenting processes and preparing reports. Actual permitted activities depend on method-level qualifications, relevant safety requirements and employer authorization. Radiation requirements apply to relevant work such as radiography, not every method.

They select, calibrate and operate ultrasonic, radiographic, magnetic particle, penetrant, eddy current and acoustic emission testing equipment according to standards and procedures, interpret signals and images, evaluate results against codes, document methods and processes and prepare inspection reports, while meeting radiation and on-site work safety requirements.
